ep-abl-055.explication: Amiodarone, which is very rich in iodine and has a long half-life, causes many adverse effects: thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism), pulmonary fibrosis or interstitial pneumonitis, liver injury, photosensitivity and blue-grey skin discoloration, corneal microdeposits and neuropathy. Regular monitoring of TSH and liver function tests, and of lung function if symptoms occur, is required. Hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia (spironolactone, digoxin) are not among its adverse effects. It also interacts with VKAs, digoxin and some statins.
ep-abl-055.aRetenir: Amiodarone: monitor thyroid, lungs, liver, skin and eyes.

ep-abl-056.question: Regarding dronedarone, which statements are correct?
options: It is contraindicated in unstable or NYHA III–IV heart failure (ANDROMEDA)
It is contraindicated in permanent AF (PALLAS)
It can cause a modest rise in creatinine by inhibiting its tubular secretion
It is the antiarrhythmic drug of choice in severe heart failure with reduced EF
commentaires: Correct: ANDROMEDA showed excess mortality in recently decompensated severe heart failure; contraindicated in unstable or NYHA III–IV HF.
Correct: PALLAS showed an excess of cardiovascular events in permanent AF.
Correct: it inhibits the tubular secretion of creatinine, which rises modestly without any real fall in filtration.
Incorrect: it is contraindicated in severe HF; amiodarone remains the antiarrhythmic drug that can be used in HFrEF.
ep-abl-056.explication: The ANDROMEDA trial was stopped because of excess mortality with dronedarone in patients with recently decompensated severe heart failure, hence the contraindication in unstable or NYHA III–IV HF. PALLAS showed an increase in cardiovascular events in permanent AF, in which it is contraindicated. In ATHENA, in paroxysmal or persistent AF, it reduced cardiovascular hospitalisation or death. It raises creatinine modestly by inhibiting its tubular secretion, without truly impairing filtration, which must be interpreted accordingly. In severe HFrEF, amiodarone remains the antiarrhythmic drug that can be used.
ep-abl-056.aRetenir: Dronedarone: never in severe/unstable HF or in permanent AF.

ep-abl-057.question: Which precaution is essential when starting sotalol?
options: Check TSH monthly for the first six months
Monitor liver function tests and lung function
None: it is used like any other beta-blocker
Monitor QT, potassium and renal function
commentaires: Incorrect: thyroid monitoring applies to amiodarone, not sotalol.
Incorrect: liver and lung monitoring apply to amiodarone.
Incorrect: its class III effect prolongs the QT in a dose-dependent manner; it is not a simple beta-blocker.
Correct: initiation with ECG monitoring of the QT, dose adjusted to renal clearance, and potassium and magnesium corrected.
ep-abl-057.explication: Sotalol combines beta-blocking activity (class II) with a class III effect (blockade of the IKr potassium current) that prolongs the QT in a dose-dependent manner: it is therefore not a beta-blocker like any other. The risk of torsades de pointes is increased by renal impairment (renal elimination), bradycardia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and female sex. It is therefore started with ECG monitoring of the QT, at a dose adjusted to creatinine clearance. Combining it with a potassium-wasting diuretic is dangerous. Thyroid, liver and lung monitoring apply to amiodarone.
ep-abl-057.aRetenir: Sotalol: monitor QT, potassium and renal function; risk of torsades.

ep-abl-058.question: In an ICD patient, which antiarrhythmic drug tends to lower the defibrillation threshold?
commentaires: Incorrect: class Ib sodium channel blockers (lidocaine, mexiletine) tend to raise the defibrillation threshold.
Correct: "pure" class III potassium channel blockers such as sotalol tend to lower the defibrillation threshold.
Incorrect: according to some data, flecainide tends rather to raise the defibrillation threshold.
Incorrect: long-term amiodarone may modestly raise the threshold, usually without consequence with current devices.
ep-abl-058.explication: Antiarrhythmic drugs that mainly block potassium currents ("pure" class III such as sotalol, or dofetilide) tend to lower the defibrillation threshold. Beta-blockers may also lower it slightly. Conversely, class Ib sodium channel blockers (lidocaine, mexiletine) tend to raise it, as does flecainide according to some data; propafenone has little effect. Long-term amiodarone may modestly raise the defibrillation threshold, although this is not usually significant with current devices. After starting or increasing an antiarrhythmic drug in an ICD patient, programming should therefore be reviewed (detection zones, as the VT rate may be slowed) and, if necessary, the safety margin checked.
ep-abl-058.aRetenir: Sotalol lowers the defibrillation threshold; amiodarone, lidocaine and mexiletine tend to raise it.

ep-abl-059.question: True or false: class Ic antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) can raise pacing thresholds, which justifies a pacemaker check after they are started in a patient with a device.
commentaires: Correct: by slowing conduction and reducing excitability, class Ic drugs can raise capture thresholds; these should be rechecked.
Incorrect: the statement is true; threshold rises on class Ic drugs are documented, especially at high doses or with hyperkalaemia; a check is prudent.
ep-abl-059.explication: Class Ic sodium channel blockers slow conduction and reduce myocardial excitability, which can raise capture thresholds, especially at high doses or with concomitant hyperkalaemia. In a pacemaker-dependent patient, loss of capture can have serious consequences. It is therefore prudent to check thresholds after starting the drug or increasing the dose, and to keep an adequate safety margin (or to use automatic capture management algorithms). In ICD patients, flecainide can also raise the defibrillation threshold (propafenone appears to have little effect on this threshold).
ep-abl-059.aRetenir: Class Ic drug started in a patient with a device: recheck pacing thresholds.

ep-abl-060.question: What is the "pill-in-the-pocket" strategy with flecainide, and what are its conditions?
ep-abl-060.reponseAttendue: A single oral dose of flecainide self-administered by the patient at the onset of an AF episode (200 mg if < 70 kg, 300 mg if ≥ 70 kg), combined with an AV nodal blocking agent, in a patient without structural heart disease who has infrequent episodes, after a first dose has been tested under monitoring in hospital.
ep-abl-060.explication: This strategy allows pharmacological cardioversion outside hospital, avoiding emergency department visits. It is reserved for patients without ischaemic heart disease or LV dysfunction, without significant conduction disease, and with infrequent, well-tolerated episodes. The first dose must be taken under monitoring to confirm efficacy and the absence of proarrhythmia or post-conversion bradycardia. A beta-blocker or rate-slowing calcium channel blocker is added to limit the risk of 1:1 conducted flutter. The patient should seek medical attention if the episode persists or is poorly tolerated.
ep-abl-060.aRetenir: Pill-in-the-pocket: single dose of flecainide 200–300 mg, structurally normal heart, first dose tested under monitoring.

ep-abl-061.question: True or false: sotalol has both beta-blocking (class II) and class III properties.
commentaires: Correct: the l-isomer carries the beta-blocking activity, and both isomers block IKr (class III), hence bradycardia and QT prolongation.
Incorrect: the statement is true; sotalol is not a pure beta-blocker; its class III effect explains the risk of torsades.
ep-abl-061.explication: Sotalol is a racemic mixture: the l-isomer carries most of the beta-blocking activity, while both isomers block the IKr potassium current (class III effect), prolonging repolarisation and the QT interval. It therefore combines bradycardia and QT prolongation, two factors that promote torsades de pointes. For this reason its use in AF is now more restricted and requires close monitoring. Amiodarone also has multiple properties (classes I, II, III and IV).
ep-abl-061.aRetenir: Sotalol = beta-blocker + class III, hence the risk of torsades.

ep-abl-062.question: Which drug is one of the first-line rate-control agents for the ventricular rate in AF?
commentaires: Incorrect: mexiletine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic drug used for ventricular arrhythmias.
Incorrect: ivabradine acts on the sinus node, not the AV node; it does not slow the ventricular response in AF.
Correct: beta-blockers such as bisoprolol slow AV nodal conduction; they are first-line rate-control agents.
Incorrect: flecainide controls rhythm, not rate; used alone, it can even accelerate the ventricular response.
ep-abl-062.explication: According to the 2024 ESC AF guidelines, first-line rate control relies on beta-blockers (bisoprolol, metoprolol, etc.), rate-slowing calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, reserved for patients with LVEF > 40%) or digoxin, depending on the patient's profile. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines advise against verapamil and diltiazem in all HFrEF, now defined as LVEF < 50%, and place beta-blockers first line in this setting. These drugs slow conduction through the AV node. Flecainide is a rhythm-control antiarrhythmic drug, not a rate-control agent, and can even accelerate the ventricular response if used alone. Mexiletine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic drug used for ventricular arrhythmias. Ivabradine acts on the sinus node, not the AV node.
ep-abl-062.aRetenir: Rate control in AF: beta-blocker, rate-slowing calcium channel blocker (if no HFrEF) or digoxin; class I antiarrhythmic drugs are not rate-control agents.

ep-abl-063.question: According to the 2024 ESC guidelines, in which situation may percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion be considered?
options: Patient preference, as a first-line alternative
Paroxysmal AF with a CHA₂DS₂-VA score of 0
commentaires: Correct: the 2024 ESC guidelines allow it to be considered (class IIb) in patients with a contraindication to long-term anticoagulation.
Incorrect: in a patient who can take an anticoagulant, occlusion does not replace it as first-line therapy.
Incorrect: with a score of 0, no thromboembolic prevention is indicated.
Incorrect: successful ablation justifies neither appendage occlusion nor stopping anticoagulation.
ep-abl-063.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines state that percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion may be considered (class IIb) in patients with AF who have a contraindication to long-term oral anticoagulation, to prevent ischaemic stroke. It does not replace first-line anticoagulation in a patient who can take it. A score of 0 does not justify any thromboembolic prevention. Surgical appendage occlusion, as an adjunct to anticoagulation, is recommended in patients undergoing cardiac surgery (LAAOS III), which is a different situation.
ep-abl-063.aRetenir: Percutaneous appendage occlusion: for patients who cannot take long-term anticoagulation.

ep-abl-064.question: What are the two main things to look for on follow-up imaging (TOE or CT) a few weeks after percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion?
ep-abl-064.reponseAttendue: 1) Device-related thrombus, which requires antithrombotic therapy to be resumed or intensified. 2) Peri-device (residual) leak, assessing its size (a large leak, classically > 5 mm, is considered significant). The position and stability of the device and the absence of effusion are also checked.
ep-abl-064.explication: After appendage occlusion, follow-up imaging is usually performed between 6 weeks and 3 months. Device-related thrombus is associated with an increased risk of stroke and requires the antithrombotic regimen to be adjusted. Peri-device leaks are common; large leaks are associated with an excess of thromboembolic events. Antithrombotic therapy after implantation depends on the device and on bleeding risk (for example, short-term anticoagulation, or dual antiplatelet therapy followed by aspirin alone). The result of this imaging guides simplification of the regimen.
ep-abl-064.aRetenir: After appendage occlusion: look for device-related thrombus and significant peri-device leak.

ep-abl-065.question: True or false: the LAAOS III trial showed that surgical left atrial appendage occlusion, performed during cardiac surgery in patients with AF, allows oral anticoagulation to be stopped without increasing the risk of stroke.
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is wrong; in LAAOS III most patients remained anticoagulated; occlusion reduced stroke as an adjunct, not as a replacement.
Correct: surgical occlusion reduces ischaemic stroke (4.8% vs 7.0%) on top of anticoagulation, which it does not replace.
ep-abl-065.explication: The statement is false. LAAOS III randomised 4811 patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication to surgical left atrial appendage occlusion or no occlusion. After a mean follow-up of 3.8 years, occlusion reduced the risk of ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism (4.8% vs 7.0%), while most patients remained on anticoagulation. The trial therefore did not evaluate stopping anticoagulation: occlusion is an adjunct, not a substitute. The 2024 ESC guidelines recommend this surgical occlusion in patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery, with anticoagulation continued according to the risk score.
ep-abl-065.aRetenir: LAAOS III: surgical appendage occlusion in addition to (not instead of) anticoagulation = fewer strokes.

ep-abl-066.question: Immediately after AV junction ablation, at what lower rate is the pacemaker classically programmed for the first few weeks?
commentaires: Incorrect: a low rate from the outset promotes QT prolongation and torsades after junction ablation.
Incorrect: 60 to 70 bpm is still insufficient during the first few weeks; the risk of torsades persists.
Correct: 80 to 90 bpm for the first few weeks (often 1 to 2 months), followed by gradual reduction, prevents torsades.
Incorrect: such a high permanent rate would be excessive and harmful.
ep-abl-066.explication: Early sudden deaths have been reported after AV junction ablation, attributed to repolarisation abnormalities (QT prolongation) promoted by the abrupt bradycardia and the change in activation sequence, with a risk of torsades de pointes. To limit this risk, the lower rate is programmed at 80 to 90 bpm for the first few weeks (often 1 to 2 months), then gradually reduced. A low rate (40 to 70 bpm) from the outset is therefore not advisable. A rate of 110 to 120 bpm would be excessive and harmful. Rate response is usually activated afterwards.
ep-abl-066.aRetenir: After AV junction ablation: lower rate 80–90 bpm initially to prevent torsades.

ep-abl-067.question: Which pacing mode and type of pacing should be favoured in a patient with permanent AF and reduced LVEF who is a candidate for AV junction ablation (ablate and pace)?
ep-abl-067.reponseAttendue: A ventricular mode without atrial sensing (VVIR; an atrial lead serves no purpose in permanent AF), with physiological pacing that avoids the dyssynchrony of pure RV pacing: biventricular resynchronisation (CRT) or conduction system pacing (preferably left bundle branch area, or His bundle with a back-up lead), depending on local expertise.
ep-abl-067.explication: After AV junction ablation, the patient becomes 100% pacemaker-dependent. Pure RV pacing causes ventricular dyssynchrony that can worsen LV function, especially if it is already impaired. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend CRT rather than RV pacing in patients with reduced LVEF who are candidates for AV junction ablation. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines recommend considering AV junction ablation combined with CRT (class IIa, level B1) in highly symptomatic, poorly controlled permanent AF with at least one HF hospitalisation. The 2025 ESC consensus on conduction system pacing considers it a reasonable option in this indication regardless of LVEF, with a preference for LBBAP (or His bundle pacing with a back-up ventricular lead). In permanent AF, an atrial lead is of no use; the mode is VVIR (or the biventricular equivalent). It is often advised to implant the device before the ablation to confirm lead stability.
ep-abl-067.aRetenir: Ablate and pace with reduced LVEF: CRT or conduction system pacing (LBBAP preferred), in VVIR mode.

ep-abl-068.question: In an elderly patient with highly symptomatic permanent AF and a persistently fast rate despite maximum tolerated rate-control therapy, which non-pharmacological rate-control strategy can be offered?
options: Slow pathway modification to slow AV conduction
Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation, then resumption of rate-control drugs
Pacemaker implantation alone, with no ablation
AV junction ablation after pacemaker implantation
commentaires: Incorrect: AV nodal modification has been abandoned because its effect is unpredictable (AV block or inadequately controlled rate).
Incorrect: the cavotricuspid isthmus is the target for typical flutter; this line does not control the rate in AF.
Incorrect: a pacemaker alone protects against bradycardia but does not slow the fast ventricular response of AF.
Correct: ablate and pace: pacemaker implanted (often a few weeks earlier), then AV junction ablation; anticoagulation maintained.
ep-abl-068.explication: The tracing shows AF with a fast ventricular response. When pharmacological rate control fails or is not tolerated, and a rhythm control strategy is not desirable, AV junction ablation combined with pacemaker implantation (ablate and pace) provides perfect, regular rate control; the device is often implanted a few weeks before the ablation to confirm lead stability. The 2024 ESC guidelines recommend considering it in these patients. The patient becomes pacemaker-dependent, and anticoagulation must be continued according to the risk score, since AF persists. Isthmus ablation treats flutter, a pacemaker alone does not slow fast AF, and slow pathway "modification", being unpredictable, has been abandoned.
ep-abl-068.aRetenir: Permanent AF refractory to rate control: AV junction ablation + pacing, with anticoagulation maintained.
ep-abl-068.legende: Permanent AF despite a beta-blocker and digoxin

ep-abl-069.question: How is the left atrium usually accessed for AF ablation?
options: Femoral artery, then retrograde aortic route
commentaires: Incorrect: the retrograde aortic route leads to the left ventricle; it does not allow practical work in the left atrium.
Correct: the catheters are advanced via the inferior vena cava, then puncture of the fossa ovalis gives access to the left atrium.
Incorrect: the coronary sinus is used as a landmark and for recording, not for access to the left atrium.
Incorrect: the epicardial approach is reserved for some VT ablations.
ep-abl-069.explication: AF ablation is performed via femoral venous access: the catheters are advanced through the inferior vena cava to the right atrium, then transseptal puncture (at the fossa ovalis) gives access to the left atrium. This puncture is often guided by echocardiography (intracardiac or transoesophageal) and fluoroscopy. The retrograde aortic arterial approach leads to the left ventricle and does not allow practical work in the left atrium. The coronary sinus, cannulated via the femoral or subclavian route, serves as a landmark and for recording. The epicardial approach is reserved for some VT ablations.
ep-abl-069.aRetenir: AF ablation: femoral venous access + transseptal puncture.

ep-abl-070.question: What is the main benefit of a 3D electroanatomical mapping system during ablation?
options: Combining 3D anatomy, electrical signals and catheter position
Delivering and titrating ablation energy at the tissue interface
Continuously measuring LVEF and intracardiac pressures
Eliminating all use of fluoroscopy during the procedure
commentaires: Correct: the map reconstructs the chambers, projects activation and voltage onto them and localises the catheter in real time, with less fluoroscopy.
Incorrect: the energy comes from a separate generator; the mapping system does not deliver it.
Incorrect: electroanatomical mapping measures neither ventricular function nor pressures.
Incorrect: it greatly reduces fluoroscopy but does not always eliminate it (transseptal puncture, positioning).
ep-abl-070.explication: 3D mapping systems (CARTO, EnSite, Rhythmia) reconstruct a virtual anatomy of the chambers and project electrical information onto it: local activation times, voltage, fractionation. They localise the catheter in real time, which makes it possible to tag ablation points, return precisely to a site and greatly reduce X-ray exposure, although not always eliminate it. They do not deliver the energy, which comes from a separate generator, and do not measure ventricular function. They are particularly useful for complex circuits (atypical flutters, scar-related VT).
ep-abl-070.aRetenir: 3D mapping = anatomy + electrical data + catheter localisation, with less fluoroscopy.

ep-abl-071.question: What is the most common, though usually benign, complication of an ablation procedure via femoral access?
options: Complete AV block requiring a pacemaker
commentaires: Incorrect: tamponade is serious but less common (around 1% in AF ablation).

ep-abl-072.question: A young woman has recurrent episodes of this tachycardia, with abrupt onset and offset. The EP study confirms typical AVNRT. What is the treatment of choice to prevent recurrence?
commentaires: Incorrect: a pacemaker has no role; AVNRT is not a bradycardia.
Incorrect: the cavotricuspid isthmus is the target for typical flutter, not AVNRT.
Incorrect: long-term amiodarone is not justified in a young patient, given its toxicity.
Correct: slow pathway ablation cures more than 95% of AVNRT, with a risk of AV block below 1% (class I).
ep-abl-072.explication: The tracing shows a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at around 180/min with no visible P wave, typical of AVNRT (retrograde P wave hidden within the QRS). For recurrent symptomatic AVNRT, slow pathway ablation has a class I recommendation in the 2019 ESC guidelines: it is curative in more than 95% of cases, with a risk of AV block below 1%. Long-term amiodarone is not justified in a young patient, given its adverse effects. A pacemaker has no role, and the cavotricuspid isthmus relates to flutter.
ep-abl-072.aRetenir: Recurrent symptomatic AVNRT: slow pathway ablation, the curative treatment of choice.

ep-abl-073.question: True or false: after AV junction ablation for permanent AF, oral anticoagulation can be stopped since the ventricular rate is controlled.
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is wrong; junction ablation only controls the ventricular response; the atria remain in AF and the embolic risk persists.
Correct: AF persists, and anticoagulation continues according to CHA₂DS₂-VA.
ep-abl-073.explication: AV junction ablation controls only the ventricular response: the atria remain in AF and the thromboembolic risk is unchanged. Anticoagulation must therefore be continued according to the CHA₂DS₂-VA score. This is a common misconception among patients, who feel much better and believe they are "cured" of their AF. It should also be remembered that these patients become pacemaker-dependent, which has implications for follow-up and programming.
ep-abl-073.aRetenir: Ablate and pace: AF persists, and so does anticoagulation.
